section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Language
section_1.content: Introduce binary (base-2) as a system using only 0 and 1. Use the visual of a light switch (Off=0, On=1) to explain how numbers are represented by place values (powers of 2).

section_2.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
section_2.content: Introduce the puzzle: 3 rods and n disks of different sizes. Rules: move one disk at a time, never place a larger disk on a smaller one. Goal: Move all disks to the target rod.
section_2.example: A 3-disk stack. The minimum moves required is 2^n - 1. For 3 disks: 2^3 - 1 = 7 moves.

section_3.title: Mapping Moves to Binary
section_3.content: Explain the elegant connection: The binary sequence of numbers from 1 to 2^n - 1 tells us exactly which disk to move at each step. If the number of the step is written in binary, the position of the rightmost '1' indicates the disk number (starting from 1).
section_3.example: For 3 disks, step 3 is '011' in binary. The rightmost '1' is at the 1st position, meaning we move the smallest disk (Disk 1).

section_4.title: Visualizing the Sequence
section_4.content: Use a synchronized animation timeline. The left side shows the binary counter incrementing (001, 010, 011...), and the right side shows the physical movement of the disks on the rods.
section_4.example: Show a robot arm moving Disk 1 on odd steps and the next available disk on even steps, following the binary 'bit-flip' pattern.

section_5.title: Synthesis & Conclusion
section_5.content: Summarize how binary is not just for computers but is the 'DNA' of recursive algorithms. Reiterate that complex puzzles are often just simplified logic patterns hidden in plain sight.
section_5.example: A final visual: A clock-like device where the 'Binary Gears' automatically solve the Towers of Hanoi as the counter ticks forward.
